Roles and responsibilities
Which of these is a RESPONSIBILITY of a guide, rather than a role?
The safety of the guests
Creating a sense of awe and wonder
Giving informative wildlife commentary
Creating a wilderness experience
The manual lists the safety of guests, working within the laws and protocols, and upholding the code of ethics as a guide's responsibilities.
Roles and responsibilities
Which of these is a ROLE of a guide, rather than a responsibility?
Creating a wilderness experience for guests
Upholding the Botswana code of ethics
Operating within the laws of the area
Ensuring the safety of the guests
The roles of a guide are to create a wilderness experience, give interesting commentary and create a sense of awe and wonder.
Briefings
Why is it useful to know and use your guests' names?
It lets you direct instructions to specific guests
It allows you to shorten the safety briefing
It is required by the Tourism Act
It helps you choose the route for the drive
Using names puts guests at ease and lets you direct instructions to specific guests, which is especially important in emergencies.
Pre-activity briefing
When can many of the pre-activity briefing points be covered?
At dinner the night before or at morning tea
Only once the game drive has started
At the first sighting of the drive
After the activity has ended
The manual says many points can be covered beforehand in the lodge, at dinner the night before or at tea on the morning of the activity.
Pre-activity briefing
Why should guests be asked to tell you about medical conditions in private?
Some may be embarrassed to share them in front of others
The law forbids discussing them in public
Other guests may then cancel the activity
The lodge manager must be present
Ask guests to see you in private after the briefing, as some people may be embarrassed to share these in front of others.
Pre-activity briefing
Which of these is listed in the manual as a medical condition to check for?
Sun sensitivity
Colour blindness
Short-sightedness
Fear of the dark
Listed conditions include allergies, asthma, pregnancy, back issues, disabilities and sun sensitivity.
Pre-activity briefing
According to the manual, what always adds great value to a guest's stay during the briefing?
Orientation against a map
A printed species checklist
A slideshow of past sightings
A tour of the lodge kitchen
Orientation against a map adds great value and lets you show how you will meet guests' expectations.
Activity brief
Where is the activity briefing best done?
On the vehicle directly before the activity
At dinner the night before
At reception when guests arrive
At the first sighting of the drive
The manual states the activity briefing is best done on the vehicle directly before an activity.
Activity brief
How should the guide explain the route and plan during the activity brief?
Using the cardinal points
Using lodge room numbers
Using GPS coordinates
Using road sign numbers
The explanation of the route and plan should be done using the cardinal points.
Activity brief
Why are guests asked not to stand while the vehicle is stationary at a sighting?
They may disturb the animal and cause it to move away
It makes the vehicle tip over more easily
It blocks the guide's view of the road
Park rules do not allow photos while standing
Standing in a sighting may cause a disturbance, making the animal move away or show interest in the vehicle.
Activity brief
What should guests do when the guide warns of overhanging branches?
Lean into the centre of the vehicle
Push the branches away with their hands
Stand up and duck under the branches
Hold the branches until the vehicle passes
Guests should lean into the centre of the vehicle and never grab or push branches, as many trees have thorns.
Activity brief
What should guests do with rubbish during a drive?
Put it in the body of the vehicle or hand it to the guide
Throw only fruit and vegetables into the bush
Bury it at the next comfort stop
Leave it at the sighting for collection
Guests must never throw anything into the bush, even fruit or vegetables; rubbish goes into the vehicle or to the guide.
Activity brief
When may guests get off the vehicle?
Only after the guide checks the area is safe and invites them
Whenever they want to take a better photo
Whenever there are no animals in sight
Only when another vehicle is nearby
Guests stay on the vehicle at all times; the guide first ensures the area is appropriate and safe before inviting them off.
Minimising risk
In what order does a PDA's behaviour escalate?
Relaxed, alert, threatening, charging
Alert, relaxed, charging, threatening
Relaxed, threatening, alert, charging
Threatening, alert, relaxed, charging
Guides must identify the escalation of a PDA's behaviour from relaxed to alert to threatening and to charging.
Minimising risk
Which of these is listed as a way for guides to minimise risk?
Continuously assessing the sighting for escape routes
Parking other vehicles in at a sighting
Poling mokoros through deep channels
Walking through thickets to get closer
Continuously assessing the area around the sighting for escape routes is listed; the others are things to avoid.
Minimising risk
Why should a guide be aware of wind direction, the sun and noise at a sighting?
To keep the animals being viewed relaxed
To get closer than the legal distance
To find the shortest route back to camp
To attract animals towards the vehicle
Keeping as many of these factors in your favour as possible keeps the animals you are viewing relaxed.
Minimising risk
What should you do if guests are still uneasy before approaching an animal?
Explain the body language of the species
Drive closer so they see it is safe
Leave the area without telling them why
Ask them to sit on the vehicle floor
If guests are uneasy, inform them about the body language of the species so they can interpret and enjoy the sighting.
Creating a wilderness experience
At what angle should the vehicle be parked at a sighting?
10 o'clock or 2 o'clock
12 o'clock, facing straight on
6 o'clock, facing away
Side-on at 9 o'clock only
Parking at 10 or 2 o'clock gives guests the best viewing and photographic angles.
Creating a wilderness experience
What should a guide do on first arriving at a sighting?
Give guests time to absorb what they are seeing
Immediately give the scientific name
Start with a long list of facts
Tell guests to take their photos quickly
Don't blurt out facts on arrival; allow guests time to absorb the scene, take images and become curious.
Creating a wilderness experience
A good guide interprets what is in front of them as:
An example of ecological interaction
A list of interesting animal facts
A chance to use scientific names
A photographic opportunity only
A good guide interprets a sighting as ecological interaction rather than simply repeating animal facts.
Creating a wilderness experience
In the sighting technique, which question asks what behaviours the animals are showing?
WHAT
WHO
WHERE
HOW
WHAT asks what they are doing and what behaviours are being exhibited.
Creating a wilderness experience
In the sighting technique, 'How is an elephant using its trunk?' is an example of which question?
HOW
WHY
WHO
WHERE
The manual gives the elephant's trunk as the example of a HOW question.
Creating a wilderness experience
Why is care and maintenance of equipment so important?
Neglected equipment may spoil a stay or endanger lives
The guide must pay for all damaged equipment
It is the only way to get a promotion
Guests inspect the equipment before each drive
Damaged or neglected equipment may irreparably affect a guest's stay or possibly endanger their lives.
Zones of approach
In which zone is the animal relaxed and showing no interest in you?
Comfort zone
Recognition zone
Warning zone
Critical zone
In the comfort zone the animal behaves naturally, shows no interest in your presence and carries on with its life.
Zones of approach
In which zone does the animal point its ears and look with focus in your direction?
Recognition zone
Comfort zone
Warning zone
Critical zone
In the recognition zone the animal stops what it was doing and puts energy into working out your agenda.
Zones of approach
In which zone does an animal give an audible or visual warning?
Warning zone
Comfort zone
Recognition zone
Critical zone
In the warning zone the animal barks, snorts, paws the ground, thrashes vegetation or flicks its tail to warn you not to come closer.
Zones of approach
What happens in the critical zone?
The animal runs away or charges you
The animal stops feeding and stares
The animal snorts and paws the ground
The animal ignores you and keeps feeding
In the critical zone the animal responds to your advance by either running away or charging.
Zones of approach
Why can retreating from a charging animal be risky?
It can increase the animal's confidence
It always causes the vehicle to stall
It leaves the guests without a briefing
It is not allowed in national parks
Retreating can increase the confidence of a charging animal, making the charge more serious.
Zones of approach
When should you establish your escape route at a sighting?
While parking the vehicle
Only once the animal charges
After the guests have taken photos
When you leave the sighting
The predetermined escape route should be established while parking.
Radio protocols
If the other party does not answer, how many times should you call before relaying the message?
No more than twice
No more than five times
Until they answer
Only once
Do not call more than twice before relaying the message; often they can hear you but cannot respond.
Radio protocols
What does 'Stand by' mean on the radio?
Wait by the radio for further communication
The message was received and understood
The answer is yes
Come to the radio now
'Stand by' tells the person to wait by the radio for further communication.
Radio protocols
What does 'Copy that' mean on the radio?
The message was received and understood
Please repeat the message
Wait by the radio for more information
The answer is no
'Copy that' means you received and understood the message.
Radio protocols
How loud should the radio volume be?
Only loud enough for people in the front to hear
Loud enough for all guests to follow
Turned off for the whole drive
As loud as possible in open areas
The radio is a disturbance to guests and should be low enough that only people in the front can hear it.
Radio protocols
How should the radio be left when it is not in use?
On scan
Switched off
On full volume
On the lodge channel only
The manual says to leave the radio on scan when not in use.
Radio protocols
In the phonetic alphabet given in the manual, which word stands for the letter Q?
Quebec
Queen
Quantum
Quiet
The manual lists Q as Quebec.
4X4 fault finding
What is the main difference between petrol and diesel bush vehicles?
The engine and electronics
The drive train
The body and seating
The wheel bearings
The main difference is in the engine and electronics; otherwise the mechanics are very similar.
4X4 fault finding
Which part returns power to the battery to keep it charged?
The alternator
The starter motor
The transfer case
The fuel pump
The energy from the engine returns power to the battery through the alternator.
The drive train
What does the transfer case do?
Changes between high range and low range
Lets the wheels turn at different speeds
Stores power to start the vehicle
Pumps fuel to the combustion chamber
The transfer case changes from high to low range, giving much more power in deep sand or when towing.
The drive train
What does the differential allow?
Wheels on each side to turn at different speeds
The engine to start without a battery
The vehicle to change from high to low range
Fuel to pass through the filters
The differential lets the side shafts turn at different speeds, for example when going around a corner.
The drive train
What do smaller gears give you?
More speed and less power
More power and less speed
More power and more speed
Less speed and less power
Smaller gears turn faster, giving more speed and less power.
The drive train
What can happen if a wheel bearing is old, worn or dry?
It can overheat, seize and the wheel can come off
The battery will go flat overnight
The engine will run out of coolant
The clutch will lose all its pressure
A worn or dry bearing can overheat and seize, which can cause the wheel to come off at speed.
The drive train
Which vehicles need their wheel bearings checked more often?
Vehicles that regularly cross through water
Vehicles that only drive on tar roads
Vehicles that are used only at night
Vehicles with petrol engines
Vehicles crossing through water regularly need their bearings checked more often.
The electrical system
When the key is turned, power goes to the starter motor, which spins the:
Flywheel
Alternator
Propeller shaft
Fuel pump
The starter motor spins the flywheel, causing the engine to kick in.
The electrical system
In a diesel vehicle, what does the electrical system heat to help the diesel start burning?
The glow plugs
The spark plugs
The fuel filter
The radiator
In diesel vehicles the electrical system heats the glow plugs; once running, pressure ignites the diesel.
Fuel delivery
Where does the pressure that pushes fuel to the engine come from?
The fuel pump
The alternator
The fuel filter
The battery
Fuel is pushed from the tank through the fuel hose by pressure from the fuel pump.
Testing for faults
Which is one of the 3 major requirements for an engine to run?
Clean air
Brake fluid
Anti-freeze
A full spare tyre
An engine needs clean fuel at a specific pressure, clean air and an electrical current.
Testing for faults
If the engine does not turn over when you turn the key, what is the most common fault?
A flat battery or loose battery terminals
A blocked air filter
An empty fuel tank
A faulty thermostat
The most common fault is a flat battery or loose terminals; clean and tighten them and test the battery.
Testing for faults
If the starter motor turns when it is bridged, which part is faulty?
The solenoid of the starter motor
The battery
The glow plugs
The alternator
If the starter motor turns when bridged, it is the solenoid of the starter motor that is faulty.
Testing for faults
What safety check must you make before bridging the starter motor?
Make sure the vehicle is not in gear
Make sure the engine is very hot
Make sure the fuel tank is empty
Make sure the lights are switched on
People have driven the vehicle over themselves while shorting the starter; make sure it is not in gear.
Testing for faults
What is a possible short-term solution for a faulty thermostat?
Remove the thermostat
Add more brake fluid
Disconnect the battery
Blow out the fuel filter
Removing the thermostat is a short-term solution, but it should be replaced so the engine runs at the right temperature.
Testing for faults
What often blocks the fins of a radiator in the bush?
Grass seeds
Brake fluid
Diesel residue
Battery acid
Radiator fins often get blocked by grass seeds, which are best blown out with a compressor.
Clutch and brake systems
If there is no pressure when you press the brake or clutch, what does it mean?
The fluid has run out or air is in the system
The battery is flat
The thermostat has failed
The wheel bearings are dry
No pressure means either the fluid has run out or air has got into the system.
Clutch and brake systems
After fixing a leak and refilling, what must you do before the brakes or clutch will work?
Bleed the system to get the air out
Remove the thermostat
Bridge the starter motor
Change the fuel filter
You must 'bleed' the brake or clutch to get the air out of the system before it will function again.
Ethics
Unless on a planned walk, how far from the vehicle may guests be, as per the Act?
Not more than 100 m
Not more than 50 m
Not more than 200 m
Not more than 500 m
As per the Act, guests should not be more than 100 m from the vehicle unless on a planned walking excursion.
Ethics
What is the closest you may park to an animal and to a den?
15 m from an animal and 30 m from a den
30 m from an animal and 15 m from a den
10 m from an animal and 20 m from a den
20 m from an animal and 50 m from a den
Never park closer than 15 m to an animal and 30 m from a den.
Ethics
How many vehicles should you try to restrict a sighting to?
Try to restrict the number of vehicles to 3 at any one sighting.
Ethics
Which of these is listed as a sensitive animal?
Bat-eared fox
Impala
Elephant
Buffalo
Sensitive animals include cheetah, wild dog, bat-eared fox, caracal, serval, aardwolf, pangolin and others.
Ethics
How should you approach a sensitive animal?
At an angle, not head-on
Head-on and quickly
From behind, with the engine revving
Head-on, but with the engine off
Continue to assess its mood and do not approach head-on but rather at an angle.
Ethics
What should you do if a sensitive animal shows signs of agitation?
Shut off the engine and, if appropriate, retreat
Drive closer so guests get a better view
Hoot to calm the animal down
Rev the engine to warn it away
If the animal shows agitation, shut off the engine immediately and, if appropriate, retreat out of the sighting.
Ethics
When predators are chasing prey, when may you start your vehicle?
Only when the hunt is over
As soon as the chase begins
When the prey runs past the vehicle
Whenever the guests ask you to
Remain still while the animal is in pursuit and only start your vehicle when the hunt is concluded.
Ethics
Which predator does the manual say is especially easily scared off its kills?
Cheetah
Lion
Spotted hyaena
Leopard
The manual says cheetah, in particular, are easily scared off their kills.
Ethics
What happens if wild dog are forced to move their den?
The chance of pup mortality increases
The pack immediately splits up
They move into a national park
The pups are weaned earlier
Wild dog are very sensitive; if forced to move a den, the chance of pup mortality is significantly increased.
Ethics
What should you do instead of making a new track around mud or sand?
Engage diff-lock and use the existing track
Drive around it on the grass
Turn back and take another route
Wait for the area to dry out
Do not make new tracks; rather engage diff-lock and use the existing track.
Ethics
What should be done with a road formed by a temporary sighting such as a carcass?
Close it when the predators have finished feeding
Keep it open for future game drives
Mark it on the lodge map
Leave it for the rangers to close
If a road is formed by a temporary sighting, close it when the predators have finished feeding.
Culture shock
What is culture shock?
Shock at unexpected behaviour from another culture
Fear of dangerous animals on a first safari
Discomfort caused by the Botswana heat
Tiredness after a long international flight
Culture shock is being shocked by an unexpected gesture or behaviour due to a lack of exposure to other cultures.
Culture shock
According to the manual, how do Japanese people greet each other?
They bow
They shake hands
They hug
They kiss on the cheek
Japanese do not shake hands to greet but rather bow to each other.
Culture shock
Which topic should a guide avoid to prevent offending guests?
Politics
Bird identification
The weather
Local food
Topics to avoid include religion, politics, racial issues, sexist remarks, homosexuality and previous wars.
Table manners
When should a guide serve themselves at a meal?
Last
First
Before the children
Before the lodge manager
Guides should always serve themselves or be served last.
Table manners
In which order should cutlery be used?
From the outside in
From the inside out
Only the fork, for every course
Whichever is closest to the plate
Use utensils from the outside in, starting with the outermost for the first course.
Table manners
Where should the napkin go once the meal is over?
Folded neatly on the side of the plate
Left on your chair
Placed on top of your food
Kept on your lap
Once the meal is over, the napkin should be folded neatly on the side of the plate.
Table manners
What does the manual say is one of a guide's roles during a meal?
Ensuring pleasant conversation
Serving the guests' food
Clearing the table
Choosing the wine for guests
One of our roles as a guide is to entertain guests by ensuring there is pleasant conversation during the meal.
